turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Morning. Dr Shah will see you in a minute. I'll just pop the cuff on for your blood pressure, alright?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm, yes. Sorry, that telly out there, I can't hear myself think.
[SEG0003] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Loud, isn't it. Right, 132 over 84, pulse 78. Through you go.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Shah. Have a seat. What's brought you in today?

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my skin. I've got this awful itchy rash between my fingers and round my waist, where the waistband rubs. It's been about three weeks, maybe a bit longer, and it's driving me mad.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. When you say three weeks, has it been there the whole time?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, yes, the whole time. I kept thinking I've overdone it at the cafe with all the hand washing, but this isn't just dry skin.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): And is there a time of day it's worse?

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Nights. After tea I'm climbing the walls. It's like something's crawling under the skin between my fingers, and there's a bit on the inside of my wrists now too. I barely sleep.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Can you see spots, or is it only the itch?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Little bumps, and I've scratched it raw in places. Same along the waist.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is anyone else in the house itching?

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. My partner Tom is scratching his wrists. And our little boy, he's four, he's itchy at bedtime as well. I'm frightened I've given it to them. We keep the place clean, honestly.

[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hmm, let me think this through. Fingers, waist, wrists, worse at night, and the people you live with itching too. That is very likely scabies. The mite sits in the skin, which is that crawling feeling.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Scabies? Oh god. Does that mean we're dirty? I hoover every single day.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): No, it doesn't mean that at all. It spreads by close skin contact, and tidy houses get it just the same.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I still work? I'm in a cafe, hands on everything. And can he go to nursery, or do I have to keep him off?
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): After the cream has gone on, you can be back at work the next day, and he can be back at nursery the next day. We'll go through it step by step so it isn't a muddle.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Is it that permetrin cream I read about? How do I even put it on?
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Permethrin five percent cream, often sold as Lyclear. You apply it from the neck downwards, all over, and leave it on for eight to twelve hours.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Not my face? What about under my nails, I bite them. And, umm, down below, do I have to?
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Leave the face unless it's itchy there. Do go under the nails, between the fingers, the soles, the groin and the bottom. Is your scalp itchy?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Scalp's fine. Face isn't itchy either. It's the hands and the waist.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Have a shower, dry off, then put the cream on cool skin. Leave it overnight and wash it off in the morning. Everybody at home should do it on the same night.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Even a four year old, the same night? Is that safe? I've read scary things online.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, it's the treatment we use from two months of age. You or Tom put it on him, neck down. Then all of you repeat the exact same thing seven days later.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I miss a patch, say behind a knee? Does it all fail? And does it sting? I'm going to mess it up.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): It can tingle a little. Try not to miss hands, wrists, waist, feet and the groin. If you've been careful, you don't throw the whole thing out over one small gap.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the bedding? There's a mountain of it. I'm all over the place trying to think it through.

[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Wash clothes and bedding from the last three days at sixty degrees. Anything that won't wash, bag it for seventy-two hours. Don't buy insecticide sprays for the sofa, they aren't needed.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Seventy-two hours for his rabbit as well, the soft toy? And all the towels?
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, bag the soft toy or hot wash it. Towels from those three days too. The mites die off the body quite quickly, so it isn't the whole house.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I did try Canesten from the chemist last week, the antifungal one. I thought it was a sweat rash. It did nothing at all.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's clotrimazole, so it was never going to clear this. You can stop it. Anything else you've put on the skin?

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I put the yellow steroid cream on, the hydrocortisone, twice last week, then I stopped because it wasn't doing much. And I take my water tablet every morning, the bendro, two point five, for my blood pressure. Years, that's been.
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Carry on with the bendroflumethiazide as usual. Hydrocortisone might ease the itch a touch but it won't kill the mites. Any allergies to medicines or creams?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Oh, and last autumn they did a cholesterol blood test, and the nurse said it was borderline. They never started me on anything.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): We won't go into that today, I haven't got a figure in front of me. Any fever while this has been going on? Any cough, or trouble breathing?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. No cough. Breathing's alright actually. I just feel like a wet rag from not sleeping.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a look. Yes, small burrows between the fingers, and scratch marks where the waistband sits. No sign of a spreading skin infection.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Are those little lines the burrows? If I'm still itching in a fortnight, has it failed? I can't keep going like this.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): The itch often carries on for two or three weeks after the mites are dead, so a fortnight doesn't mean it failed. If the rash is still spreading after the second treatment, or if you see pus, or you feel feverish, come back sooner. Otherwise I'll see you in four weeks.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. And Tom and our boy definitely treat the same night, even if his spots are tiny? How much cream do we get?

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Same night, all three of you, whether you can see much or not. I'll prescribe three tubes of permethrin five percent to start with. You repeat it on day seven, so check with the chemist whether you'll need more cream for that second go. Reception can book the four week visit.
[SEG0045] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Pop out to me when you're done and I'll book the four weeks. The prescription usually hits the chemist next door within the hour.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you. Sorry for firing questions. I'll write every step down so I don't lose them.

social_history.description: lives with partner and four-year-old son

clinical_actions.description: Prescribe three tubes of permethrin 5% cream, applied once and repeated after 7 days

Partner and son to be treated with the same cream on the same night, repeated after 7 days
Hot wash clothes, bedding and towels from the last 3 days at 60 degrees, and bag unwashable items including soft toys for 72 hours
Do not use insecticide sprays on the sofa
Patient may return to cafe work and the child to nursery the day after the cream is applied
Itch may continue for 2 to 3 weeks after the mites are dead and this does not by itself mean treatment failed

time_reference.value: if the rash is still spreading after the second treatment, or if you see pus, or you feel feverish

spec.situation: Itchy rash between fingers and at the waist, worse at night, partner and child also itch; permethrin cream explained step by step; household treatment and washing advice.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

bad.reason: Doctor notes scratch marks where waistband sits; exact body site stated as waistband, not simply waist.
Cholesterol blood test was completed, but transcript doesn't say patient requested it.

omissions.text: Patient reported little bumps and that she had scratched the rash raw in places; these lesion details are not recorded.
Negative finding: face is not itchy.
Permethrin application instruction was to leave the face untreated unless it is itchy there.
Permethrin should be applied after a shower, to cool dry skin, left on overnight, and washed off in the morning.
Doctor advised permethrin can tingle/sting a little.
Medication detail missing: patient used hydrocortisone only twice last week before stopping.
Doctor advised to continue bendroflumethiazide as usual.
Past investigation result detail missing: cholesterol blood test last autumn was reported as borderline, and no treatment was started.
